title: Why the national curriculum is not as important as you think
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou argues that England's national curriculum, though important, is a weak lever for changing what students learn. The document runs to about 300 pages and leaves enormous decisions, such as how long to spend on a topic, to schools, publishers and teachers. She names four other parts of the system that matter more: lesson resources, teachers and their training, inspection, and assessment. Assessment especially makes the curriculum concrete, yet most of the national curriculum is never assessed. Her conclusion is that rewriting the words in the document will not alone make much difference. It sits in Learning & Curriculum because it is about curriculum design and the assessment that makes it real.
points: The national curriculum does not tell teachers what to teach each lesson; huge interpretive work falls to schools and resource creators.
Resources only succeed if teachers are trained in and believe in them, which is why strong systems integrate resources into teacher training.
Inspection is one imperfect check on whether schools teach the curriculum at all.
Assessment is the bridge between teaching and learning and makes a curriculum concrete, yet most of the curriculum is never externally assessed.
Politicians who want to change what students learn will not do it by revising a 300-page document.
quotes: I have written a lot about the curriculum and I think it's an important part of education. But I also think that the national curriculum in England - and many other countries - is not as important as is sometimes assumed.

The entire primary and secondary curriculum for every subject is about 300 pages long. A huge amount of work has to be done to turn what you see in this curriculum document into actual living and breathing lessons.
Schools can choose to teach 40 minutes of history a week or three hours. These decisions make a huge difference and are entirely up to schools.

You can have the most brilliant curriculum & resources in the world, but you need teachers to deliver it, you need teachers who have had training in how to deliver it, and you need teachers who believe that it is deliverable. It is possible for extremely well-designed resources to fail in the classroom if teachers don’t understand how they work.
They don’t really care whether it is on the curriculum or not. What they care about is whether students know and can do [this important thing].

What is the conclusion for politicians and for anyone concerned with changing what students learn? Revising the words in a 300 page curriculum document will not, on its own, make much of a difference. It is a much bigger challenge.
